Yes—this changes the near-term product definition in a useful way:

`latex-ingest` should become a standalone manuscript exporter. “Oracle” becomes one use of it; “publish” remains a separate corpus workflow; the evolving JSONL ABI stays internal and optional.

### Export contract

I would make the public operation something like:

```text
latex export <source> -TargetRoot <directory> [-Slug <slug>]
```

Producing only:

```text
<target-root>/<slug>/
├── <slug>-latex.md
└── images/
    ├── figure-001-results.png
    ├── figure-002a-ablation.svg
    └── source/                 # originals retained when conversion is lossy
        └── figure-001-results.pdf
```

The default bundle should not contain `.runs`, intermediate JSONL, counts, renderer logs, patches, or temporary TeX. Diagnostics and optional IR dumps belong in the work directory or an explicitly requested location.

This corrects the current awkward contract: Markdown is written directly under `OutDir`, while assets go under `OutDir/<slug>/`, as seen in [latex-ingest.ps1](./src/latex-ingest/latex-ingest.ps1:1943) and [Copy-LatexFigures](./src/latex-ingest/latex-ingest.ps1:1742).

### A workable definition of “faithful and complete”

For Markdown, fidelity cannot mean reproducing page layout, line breaking, float placement, or journal typography. I would define it as:

> Every active manuscript construct is either represented semantically in Markdown, externalized as an asset, preserved through an explicit lossless/raw fallback, or reported as unresolved. Nothing disappears silently.

That covers:

- Title and complete front matter
- Abstract, body, headings, lists, math, theorems and algorithms
- Footnotes and acknowledgements
- Figures, subfigures, captions and empirical plots
- Tables, including a fallback for structures Markdown cannot express
- Appendices and their identity
- Labels, cross-references and numbering
- Citation intent, citation notes and bibliography
- External listings and other included text
- Explicit diagnostics for anything unsupported

The `2607.16621` result demonstrates why this definition matters: its ordinary prose is fairly good, but its authorship metadata disappears, 44 cited keys remain unresolved despite a 61-entry `.bib`, and five external listings are left as raw `\lstinputlisting` commands. Those are manuscript-completeness failures even though the Markdown looks superficially clean.

### Bibliography should be compile-assisted

The most faithful initial solution is not to hand-build a complete BibTeX implementation inside PowerShell. The exporter should run a constrained, no-shell-escape build when necessary and consume the products TeX already knows how to generate:

- `.fls` for the actual project/input and asset closure
- `.aux` for citations, labels and counters
- `.bbl` for rendered bibliography content
- `.bcf` when Biber is involved
- `.log` for missing files and undefined references

Existing `.bbl` files can be used directly. Raw `.bib` parsing remains a fallback and a source of richer metadata for the future ABI.

References should be inserted where `\bibliography` or `\printbibliography` occurs—not simply appended unconditionally—and citation commands should retain their keys, mode, prenotes and postnotes internally.

### Images need a real asset pipeline

The current image support is a promising foundation, especially its encode-first diagram handling and explicit failure markers, but it is incomplete in ways that lose content:

- `\includegraphics` is recognized with a shallow regex and its options are ignored.
- Figure-grid `tabular` blocks are collapsed to a generic marker, losing every panel. One gauntlet case turns 50 `\includegraphics` calls into 11 generic markers and zero image links.
- Recursive basename lookup can select the wrong file when names repeat.
- Basename collisions can overwrite assets.
- Nested captions remain raw.
- PDF graphics are rasterized at a fixed 200 DPI and the vector original is discarded.

The intended policy should be:

1. Semantic diagram that can be represented faithfully in KaTeX → embedded math.
2. Author-supplied plot, photograph or complex graphic → copied or converted into `images/`.
3. TikZ/picture diagram that cannot be lowered faithfully → rendered to SVG or PNG.
4. Composite figure → preserve every panel, its order, subcaption, main caption and labels.
5. Failed or missing graphic → explicit marker and an incomplete export status.

Options such as `page`, `trim`, `clip`, and `angle` affect visible content and must be applied, potentially by rendering through TeX. Width and height are primarily presentation metadata. When conversion is lossy, I would retain the original asset alongside the Markdown-compatible derivative.

### ABI development without contaminating the product

I would introduce one in-memory export model, not a procession of durable stage IRs. The initial records only need the information forced by real export requirements:

```text
id, kind, parent_id
source_file, source_span
content, attributes
labels, references, citation_keys
assets
raw_tex
status, diagnostics
```

Markdown becomes the first projection of that model. `-EmitIr` can optionally serialize it as JSONL for studying the ABI and later convergence with PDF extraction. The schema can evolve against the gauntlet without making ordinary users interact with it.

### Recommended development sequence

1. Formalize the clean bundle, work-directory separation, export result and completeness invariants.
2. Repair project resolution and add constrained compile assistance.
3. Complete front matter, citations, bibliography and external listings.
4. Build the figure/asset graph, including subfigures, grids, captions and collision-safe paths.
5. Complete appendices, labels, references, footnotes, algorithms and complex-table fallbacks.
6. Turn the gauntlet into structural acceptance tests: citation closure, input closure, asset closure and an empty unresolved-construct ledger.
7. Stabilize the observed internal model into the first ABI candidate.

The first genuinely useful vertical slice is therefore: clean bundle + completeness accounting + bibliography + image extraction. That gets you a practical exporter quickly while making each added capability teach us something concrete about the future shared ABI.

> i'm not interested in a carbon copy of the original document, i'm aiming for the latent canonical markdown manuscript that faithfully retains the content. latex->markdown is inherently lossy along some dimensions, but not really in any way that matters for binding the knowledge in markdown. in many cases the mapping involves making opinionated decisions or adopting conventions for how something that can't be literally converted to markdown has to be represented. All I want in a bibliography is a standard markdown citation list, with the numbering preserved, and maybe eventually with in-document links that can be used to automatically navigate. and this process and the contracts are exactly the kinds of things i'm trying to determine inductively by working through this end-to-end workflow, which has utility on its own merits as well as being instructive.

Right—I over-weighted reversibility and archival fidelity. Your target is a semantic projection: preserve knowledge-bearing content, while deliberately normalizing away TeX authoring mechanics and visual typesetting choices.

A better working definition is:

> A faithful export retains every meaningful manuscript assertion, relationship, structure, and supporting artifact in a consistent Markdown convention. Loss of layout or TeX implementation detail is acceptable; silent loss or distortion of knowledge is not.

That means:

- Preserve prose, math, hierarchy, theorem identity, table data, code, captions, footnotes, citations, references, appendices, and the informational content of figures.
- Normalize float placement, page layout, font commands, spacing, widths, journal styling, and other presentation machinery.
- Choose canonical representations when Markdown has no literal equivalent.
- Treat unresolved knowledge-bearing content as an exporter defect or explicit development diagnostic—not as material that must necessarily appear as raw TeX in the finished document.

For bibliography, the initial convention can be deliberately simple:

```markdown
The result follows from [7].

## References

1. A. Author. “First title.” Journal, 2022.
2. B. Author and C. Author. “Second title.” Publisher, 2023.
...
7. D. Author. “Relevant title.” Journal, 2024.
```

The essential contract is:

- Preserve bibliography order and numbering.
- Resolve every in-text citation to the appropriate number.
- Retain enough bibliographic content to identify and retrieve the work.
- Normalize away BibTeX/Biber formatting machinery.
- Later, citations can become `[7](#ref-7)` with corresponding anchors without changing the conceptual model.

Citation keys are useful internally for resolving the document, but need not appear in the canonical Markdown or become a prominent ABI concern.

The same principle simplifies images. The bundle only needs the final useful assets:

```text
<slug>/
├── <slug>-latex.md
└── images/
    ├── figure-001.png
    ├── figure-002a.svg
    └── diagram-003.png
```

There is no need to preserve original PDFs or TeX graphics merely for reversibility if the exported image faithfully communicates the intended content. The conventions can emerge case by case:

- Empirical plot or photograph → image.
- Diagram cleanly expressible as supported KaTeX → embedded math.
- Complex TikZ diagram → rendered image.
- Multi-panel figure → a canonical grouping of panel images and captions, without necessarily reproducing the original visual grid.
- Table → Markdown table when semantically adequate; another explicit convention when it is not.

This also suggests a better way to approach the ABI. It should emerge from the semantic distinctions the exporter actually needs—not from attempting to model the entire LaTeX source language. Its vocabulary will probably contain things such as sections, paragraphs, math, figures, captions, tables, code, citations and reference entries. Source spans, raw TeX and transformation histories can remain development instrumentation rather than defining the manuscript itself.

I would therefore make the process deliberately inductive:

1. Keep a functioning end-to-end Markdown exporter.
2. Select representative gauntlet failures.
3. Decide the canonical Markdown representation for each construct.
4. Implement it and add a golden fixture.
5. Record the accepted loss and preserved meaning.
6. Only promote recurring semantic requirements into the prospective ABI.

A small decision ledger would be more useful now than a prematurely fixed schema:

```text
Source construct | Canonical Markdown form | Meaning retained | Accepted loss
```

The first vertical slice still looks like bibliography plus figures, but with a much leaner goal: produce the correct normalized Markdown, learn what semantic objects were necessary to do so, and keep all development artifacts outside the clean bundle. That makes the exporter useful immediately while allowing the latent manuscript contract to reveal itself through actual cases.

> my thesis is that there is essentially a surjection of any academic paper onto a canonical latent manuscript envelope in markdown, which incidentally, structurally resembles the original manuscript format of any given paper, if that makes sense. but i'm trying to solve an ill-posed inverse problem here

Yes, that makes sense. I’d formulate the thesis as a universal many-to-one projection:

```text
latent manuscript M + presentation choices N ──generate──> artifact A
artifact A ──canonicalize/infer──> canonical Markdown [M]
```

Here, `N` includes LaTeX macros, journal styling, float placement, page geometry, bibliography machinery, and other representational choices. Many different artifacts can realize the same latent manuscript, so the canonicalization map is naturally surjective and many-to-one.

The inverse is ill-posed because the generative map is not injective:

- Different latent structures can produce indistinguishable rendered output.
- Source representations contain arbitrary implementation choices.
- PDFs erase logical boundaries and provenance.
- Markdown cannot encode every distinction directly.
- “Meaningful” versus “presentational” information is not determined mechanically.

The canonical conventions are therefore not compromises around the problem—they are the regularization that makes the inverse solvable. A standard reference list, linearized subfigures, normalized theorem blocks, KaTeX math, and rendered diagrams are all choices that select one stable representative from several semantically equivalent possibilities.

In that framing, what you are discovering inductively is really the equivalence relation:

> Which differences between two manuscript representations should count as the same latent manuscript?

The structural resemblance to the original follows naturally. Most academic papers share an underlying ordered content graph:

```text
manuscript
├── front matter
├── abstract
├── section hierarchy
│   ├── prose and mathematics
│   ├── claims, definitions and proofs
│   ├── figures and captions
│   ├── tables and code
│   └── citations
├── appendices
└── references
```

LaTeX, PDF, and canonical Markdown are different serializations or observations of that graph. The Markdown should resemble the original manuscript structurally because it preserves the graph’s order, containment, and semantic roles—not because it imitates its pages.

This also clarifies the envelope. It is not bare CommonMark; it is something like:

```text
Markdown
+ LaTeX/KaTeX mathematics
+ linked image assets
+ fenced code
+ a small set of canonical manuscript conventions
```

That escape capacity is what makes the surjection plausible. When something cannot be encoded textually without distortion, the envelope can retain it as an evidence-bearing asset with its caption and structural position.

The core success criterion is consequently semantic convergence. Given the LaTeX and PDF for the same paper:

```text
canonicalize(latex) ≈ canonicalize(pdf)
```

They need not be byte-identical, but they should contain the same claims, mathematical relationships, hierarchy, citations, reference entries, tabular facts, code, and figure evidence. Disagreement is evidence of either a converter gap or an unresolved envelope convention.

That makes the current LaTeX workflow especially useful: it is the higher-observability route for constructing provisional canonical manuscripts. The future PDF workflow can then target the same latent object. The ABI emerges from the distinctions required to explain and reconcile those outputs.

So the central research task is not finding an exact inverse. It is choosing the quotient space—and the conventions that make one canonical representative stable, useful, and knowledge-complete. The gauntlet is effectively where that equivalence relation gets discovered.

> # Context Mode: Default for All Large Output
>
> ## MANDATORY RULE
>
> <context_mode_logic>
>   <mandatory_rule>
>     Default to context-mode for ALL commands. Only use Bash for guaranteed-small-output operations.
>   </mandatory_rule>
> </context_mode_logic>
>
> Bash whitelist (safe to run directly):
> - **File mutations**: `mkdir`, `mv`, `cp`, `rm`, `touch`, `chmod`
> - **Git writes**: `git add`, `git commit`, `git push`, `git checkout`, `git branch`, `git merge`
> - **Navigation**: `cd`, `pwd`, `which`
> - **Process control**: `kill`, `pkill`
> - **Package management**: `npm install`, `npm publish`, `pip install`
> - **Simple output**: `echo`, `printf`
>
> **Everything else → `ctx_execute` or `ctx_execute_file`.** Any command that reads, queries, fetches, lists, logs, tests, builds, diffs, inspects, or calls an external service. This includes ALL CLIs (gh, aws, kubectl, docker, terraform, wrangler, fly, heroku, gcloud, etc.) — there are thousands and we cannot list them all.
>
> **When uncertain, use context-mode.** Every KB of unnecessary context reduces the quality and speed of the entire session.
>
> ## Decision Tree
>
> ```
> About to run a command / read a file / call an API?
> │
> ├── Command is on the Bash whitelist (file mutations, git writes, navigation, echo)?
> │   └── Use Bash
> │
> ├── Output MIGHT be large or you're UNSURE?
> │   └── Use context-mode ctx_execute or ctx_execute_file
> │
> ├── Fetching web documentation or HTML page?
> │   └── Use ctx_fetch_and_index → ctx_search
> │
> ├── Using Playwright (navigate, snapshot, console, network)?
> │   └── ALWAYS use filename parameter to save to file, then:
> │       browser_snapshot(filename) → ctx_index(path) or ctx_execute_file(path)
> │       browser_console_messages(filename) → ctx_execute_file(path)
> │       browser_network_requests(filename) → ctx_execute_file(path)
> │       ⚠ browser_navigate returns a snapshot automatically — ignore it,
> │         use browser_snapshot(filename) for any inspection.
> │       ⚠ Playwright MCP uses a SINGLE browser instance — NOT parallel-safe.
> │         For parallel browser ops, use agent-browser via execute instead.
> │
> ├── Using agent-browser (parallel-safe browser automation)?
> │   └── Run via execute (shell) — each call gets its own subprocess:
> │       execute("agent-browser open example.com && agent-browser snapshot -i -c")
> │       ✓ Supports sessions for isolated browser instances
> │       ✓ Safe for parallel subagent execution
> │       ✓ Lightweight accessibility tree with ref-based interaction
> │
> ├── Processing output from another MCP tool (Context7, GitHub API, etc.)?
> │   ├── Output already in context from a previous tool call?
> │   │   └── Use it directly. Do NOT re-index with ctx_index(content: ...).
> │   ├── Need to search the output multiple times?
> │   │   └── Save to file via ctx_execute, then ctx_index(path) → ctx_search
> │   └── One-shot extraction?
> │       └── Save to file via ctx_execute, then ctx_execute_file(path)
> │
> └── Reading a file to analyze/summarize (not edit)?
>     └── Use ctx_execute_file (file loads into FILE_CONTENT, not context)
> ```
>
> ## When to Use Each Tool
>
> | Situation | Tool | Example |
> |-----------|------|---------|
> | Hit an API endpoint | `ctx_execute` | `fetch('http://localhost:3000/api/orders')` |
> | Run CLI that returns data | `ctx_execute` | `gh pr list`, `aws s3 ls`, `kubectl get pods` |
> | Run tests | `ctx_execute` | `npm test`, `pytest`, `go test ./...` |
> | Git operations | `ctx_execute` | `git log --oneline -50`, `git diff HEAD~5` |
> | Docker/K8s inspection | `ctx_execute` | `docker stats --no-stream`, `kubectl describe pod` |
> | Read a log file | `ctx_execute_file` | Parse access.log, error.log, build output |
> | Read a data file | `ctx_execute_file` | Analyze CSV, JSON, YAML, XML |
> | Read source code to analyze | `ctx_execute_file` | Count functions, find patterns, extract metrics |
> | Fetch web docs | `ctx_fetch_and_index` | Index React/Next.js/Zod docs, then search |
> | Playwright snapshot | `browser_snapshot(filename)` → `ctx_index(path)` → `ctx_search` | Save to file, index server-side, query |
> | Playwright snapshot (one-shot) | `browser_snapshot(filename)` → `ctx_execute_file(path)` | Save to file, extract in sandbox |
> | Playwright console/network | `browser_*(filename)` → `ctx_execute_file(path)` | Save to file, analyze in sandbox |
> | MCP output (already in context) | Use directly | Don't re-index — it's already loaded |
> | MCP output (need multi-query) | `ctx_execute` to save → `ctx_index(path)` → `ctx_search` | Save to file first, index server-side |
> | Wipe indexed KB content | `ctx_purge(confirm: true)` | Permanently deletes all indexed content |
>
> ## Automatic Triggers
>
> Use context-mode for ANY of these, without being asked:
>
> - **API debugging**: "hit this endpoint", "call the API", "check the response", "find the bug in the response"
> - **Log analysis**: "check the logs", "what errors", "read access.log", "debug the 500s"
> - **Test runs**: "run the tests", "check if tests pass", "test suite output"
> - **Git history**: "show recent commits", "git log", "what changed", "diff between branches"
> - **Data inspection**: "look at the CSV", "parse the JSON", "analyze the config"
> - **Infrastructure**: "list containers", "check pods", "S3 buckets", "show running services"
> - **Dependency audit**: "check dependencies", "outdated packages", "security audit"
> - **Build output**: "build the project", "check for warnings", "compile errors"
> - **Code metrics**: "count lines", "find TODOs", "function count", "analyze codebase"
> - **Web docs lookup**: "look up the docs", "check the API reference", "find examples"
>
> ## Language Selection
>
> | Situation | Language | Why |
> |-----------|----------|-----|
> | HTTP/API calls, JSON | `javascript` | Native fetch, JSON.parse, async/await |
> | Data analysis, CSV, stats | `python` | csv, statistics, collections, re |
> | Shell commands with pipes | `shell` | grep, awk, jq, native tools |
> | File pattern matching | `shell` | find, wc, sort, uniq |
>
> ## Search Query Strategy
>
> - BM25 uses **OR semantics** — results matching more terms rank higher automatically
> - Use 2-4 specific technical terms per query
> - **Always use `source` parameter** when multiple docs are indexed to avoid cross-source contamination
>   - Partial match works: `source: "Node"` matches `"Node.js v22 CHANGELOG"`
> - **Always use `queries` array** — batch ALL search questions in ONE call:
>   - `ctx_search(queries: ["transform pipe", "refine superRefine", "coerce codec"], source: "Zod")`
>   - NEVER make multiple separate ctx_search() calls — put all queries in one array
>
> ## External Documentation
>
> - **Always use `ctx_fetch_and_index`** for external docs — NEVER `cat` or `ctx_execute` with local paths for packages you don't own
> - For GitHub-hosted projects, use the raw URL: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/org/repo/main/CHANGELOG.md`
> - After indexing, use the `source` parameter in search to scope results to that specific document
>
> ## Critical Rules
>
> 1. **Always console.log/print your findings.** stdout is all that enters context. No output = wasted call.
> 2. **Write analysis code, not just data dumps.** Don't `console.log(JSON.stringify(data))` — analyze first, print findings.
> 3. **Be specific in output.** Print bug details with IDs, line numbers, exact values — not just counts.
> 4. **For files you need to EDIT**: Use the normal Read tool. context-mode is for analysis, not editing.
> 5. **For Bash whitelist commands only**: Use Bash for file mutations, git writes, navigation, process control, package install, and echo. Everything else goes through context-mode.
> 6. **Never use `ctx_index(content: large_data)`.** Use `ctx_index(path: ...)` to read files server-side. The `content` parameter sends data through context as a tool parameter — use it only for small inline text.
> 7. **Always use `filename` parameter** on Playwright tools (`browser_snapshot`, `browser_console_messages`, `browser_network_requests`). Without it, the full output enters context.
> 8. **Don't re-index data already in context.** If an MCP tool returned data in a previous response, it's already loaded — use it directly or save to file first.
>
> ## Sandboxed Data Workflow
>
> <sandboxed_data_workflow>
>   <critical_rule>
>     When using tools that support saving to a file: ALWAYS use the 'filename' parameter.
>     NEVER return large raw datasets directly to context.
>   </critical_rule>
>   <workflow>
>     LargeDataTool(filename: "path") → mcp__context-mode__ctx_index(path: "path") → ctx_search()
>   </workflow>
> </sandboxed_data_workflow>
>
> This is the universal pattern for context preservation regardless of
> the source tool (Playwright, GitHub API, AWS CLI, etc.).
>
> ## Examples
>
> ### Debug an API endpoint
> ```javascript
> const resp = await fetch('http://localhost:3000/api/orders');
> const { orders } = await resp.json();
>
> const bugs = [];
> const negQty = orders.filter(o => o.quantity < 0);
> if (negQty.length) bugs.push(`Negative qty: ${negQty.map(o => o.id).join(', ')}`);
>
> const nullFields = orders.filter(o => !o.product || !o.customer);
> if (nullFields.length) bugs.push(`Null fields: ${nullFields.map(o => o.id).join(', ')}`);
>
> console.log(`${orders.length} orders, ${bugs.length} bugs found:`);
> bugs.forEach(b => console.log(`- ${b}`));
> ```
>
> ### Analyze test output
> ```shell
> npm test 2>&1
> echo "EXIT=$?"
> ```
>
> ### Check GitHub PRs
> ```shell
> gh pr list --json number,title,state,reviewDecision --jq '.[] | "\(.number) [\(.state)] \(.title) — \(.reviewDecision // "no review")"'
> ```
>
> ### Read and analyze a large file
> ```python
> # FILE_CONTENT is pre-loaded by ctx_execute_file
> import json
> data = json.loads(FILE_CONTENT)
> print(f"Records: {len(data)}")
> # ... analyze and print findings
> ```
>
> ## Browser & Playwright Integration
>
> **When a task involves Playwright snapshots, screenshots, or page inspection, ALWAYS route through file → sandbox.**
>
> Playwright `browser_snapshot` returns 10K–135K tokens of accessibility tree data. Calling it without `filename` dumps all of that into context. Passing the output to `ctx_index(content: ...)` sends it into context a SECOND time as a parameter. Both are wrong.
>
> **The key insight**: `browser_snapshot` has a `filename` parameter that saves to file instead of returning to context. `ctx_index` has a `path` parameter that reads files server-side. `ctx_execute_file` processes files in a sandbox. **None of these touch context.**
>
> ### Workflow A: Snapshot → File → Index → Search (multiple queries)
>
> ```
> Step 1: browser_snapshot(filename: "/tmp/playwright-snapshot.md")
>         → saves to file, returns ~50B confirmation (NOT 135K tokens)
>
> Step 2: ctx_index(path: "/tmp/playwright-snapshot.md", source: "Playwright snapshot")
>         → reads file SERVER-SIDE, indexes into FTS5, returns ~80B confirmation
>
> Step 3: ctx_search(queries: ["login form email password"], source: "Playwright")
>         → returns only matching chunks (~300B)
> ```
>
> **Total context: ~430B** instead of 270K tokens. Real 99% savings.
>
> ### Workflow B: Snapshot → File → Execute File (one-shot extraction)
>
> ```
> Step 1: browser_snapshot(filename: "/tmp/playwright-snapshot.md")
>         → saves to file, returns ~50B confirmation
>
> Step 2: ctx_execute_file(path: "/tmp/playwright-snapshot.md", language: "javascript", code: "
>           const links = [...FILE_CONTENT.matchAll(/- link \"([^\"]+)\"/g)].map(m => m[1]);
>           const buttons = [...FILE_CONTENT.matchAll(/- button \"([^\"]+)\"/g)].map(m => m[1]);
>           const inputs = [...FILE_CONTENT.matchAll(/- textbox|- checkbox|- radio/g)];
>           console.log('Links:', links.length, '| Buttons:', buttons.length, '| Inputs:', inputs.length);
>           console.log('Navigation:', links.slice(0, 10).join(', '));
>         ")
>         → processes in sandbox, returns ~200B summary
> ```
>
> **Total context: ~250B** instead of 135K tokens.
>
> ### Workflow C: Console & Network (save to file if large)
>
> ```
> browser_console_messages(level: "error", filename: "/tmp/console.md")
> → ctx_execute_file(path: "/tmp/console.md", ...) or ctx_index(path: "/tmp/console.md", ...)
>
> browser_network_requests(includeStatic: false, filename: "/tmp/network.md")
> → ctx_execute_file(path: "/tmp/network.md", ...) or ctx_index(path: "/tmp/network.md", ...)
> ```
>
> ### CRITICAL: Why `filename` + `path` is mandatory
>
> | Approach | Context cost | Correct? |
> |----------|-------------|----------|
> | `browser_snapshot()` → raw into context | **135K tokens** | NO |
> | `browser_snapshot()` → `ctx_index(content: raw)` | **270K tokens** (doubled!) | NO |
> | `browser_snapshot(filename)` → `ctx_index(path)` → `ctx_search` | **~430B** | YES |
> | `browser_snapshot(filename)` → `ctx_execute_file(path)` | **~250B** | YES |
>
> ### Key Rule
>
> > **ALWAYS use `filename` parameter when calling `browser_snapshot`, `browser_console_messages`, or `browser_network_requests`.**
> > Then process via `ctx_index(path: ...)` or `ctx_execute_file(path: ...)` — never `ctx_index(content: ...)`.
> >
> > Data flow: **Playwright → file → server-side read → context**. Never: **Playwright → context → ctx_index(content) → context again**.
>
> ## Subagent Usage
>
> Subagents automatically receive context-mode tool routing via a PreToolUse hook. You do NOT need to manually add tool names to subagent prompts — the hook injects them. Just write natural task descriptions.
>
> ## Anti-Patterns
>
> - Using `curl http://api/endpoint` via Bash → 50KB floods context. Use `ctx_execute` with fetch instead.
> - Using `cat large-file.json` via Bash → entire file in context. Use `ctx_execute_file` instead.
> - Using `gh pr list` via Bash → raw JSON in context. Use `ctx_execute` with `--jq` filter instead.
> - Piping Bash output through `| head -20` → you lose the rest. Use `ctx_execute` to analyze ALL data and print summary.
> - Narrowing `ctx_execute` output upstream of capture → `ctx_execute` captures, `ctx_search` filters; merging the layers drops data that the index never sees. See `references/anti-patterns.md` §8.
> - Running `npm test` via Bash → full test output in context. Use `ctx_execute` to capture and summarize.
> - Calling `browser_snapshot()` WITHOUT `filename` parameter → 135K tokens flood context. **Always** use `browser_snapshot(filename: "/tmp/snap.md")`.
> - Calling `browser_console_messages()` or `browser_network_requests()` WITHOUT `filename` → entire output floods context. **Always** use the `filename` parameter.
> - Passing ANY large data to `ctx_index(content: ...)` → data enters context as a parameter. **Always** use `ctx_index(path: ...)` to read server-side. The `content` parameter should only be used for small inline text you're composing yourself.
> - Calling an MCP tool (Context7 `query-docs`, GitHub API, etc.) then passing the response to `ctx_index(content: response)` → **doubles** context usage. The response is already in context — use it directly or save to file first.
> - Ignoring `browser_navigate` auto-snapshot → navigation response includes a full page snapshot. Don't rely on it for inspection — call `browser_snapshot(filename)` separately.
> - Expecting `ctx_stats` to reset or wipe anything → `ctx_stats` is read-only (shows stats only). Use `ctx_purge(confirm: true)` to permanently delete all indexed content.
>

>   28: The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we give a brief description of distance measures between network objects. Based on Laplacian flow, we propose a novel distance measure, characterize its properties, and provide an efficient numerical scheme in Section 3. Our simulation in Section 4 supports our new proposal to outperform incumbent metrics.
>   29:
>   30: ## 2. Related Work
>   31:
>   32: Let G be a network or graph with $n$ nodes with its adjacency matrix A , which is an n × n matrix. For a binary network, $A_{ij}$ = 1 if node i and j has an observed edge between two nodes and $A_{ij}$ = 0 otherwise for 1 ≤ i,j ≤ n . The graph Laplacian of a graph G is defined as L = D − A , where D is a degree matrix such that $D_{ii}$ = j $A_{ij}$ for 1 ≤ i ≤ n and $D_{ij}$ = 0 otherwise [30].
>   33:
>   34: Several measures have been proposed to describe dissimilarity based on direct observables of the network. One simple way is to count the number of matching edges from two networks [13], the popular Hamming distance. In [31], Wilson and Zhu suggested to use the Euclidean distance between the spectra of two adjacency matrices. From a network-theoretic perspective, Roy et al. [26] claimed the discrepancy of node-defined centrality measures be a candidate for dissimilarity measure.
>   35:
>   36: The graph Laplacian has been known as an approximation of the LaplaceBeltrami operator on smooth manifold underlying observed objects [11]. Since L contains geometric and topological information of the data via its spectrum, many strategies have been proposed.
>   37:
>   38: Since the graph Laplacian matrix is symmetric and positive-semidefinite, eigenvalues of L are nonnegative real numbers. Jakobson and Rivin exploited such phenomenon by defining the distance measure by taking normalized sum of squared differences for top eigenvalues [17]. Instead of using eigenvalues directly, some chose to compute the disparity of two approximated distributions of spectrum. Ipsen and Mikhailov, in [16], suggested to apply kernel density estimation by convolving narrow Lorentz distributions with computed eigenvalues, while Fay et al. employed discrete histogram through binning [7].
>   39:

Section 3 develops the Riemannian Gaussian model and the weighted maximum likelihood problem. Section 4 introduces finite mixtures and the exact and generalized EM algorithms. Section 5 establishes the main existence, uniqueness, and monotonicity results. >   68: We collect the geometric notation and analytic conventions used throughout the paper. Unless stated otherwise, hyperbolic space is taken to have constant sectional curvature of −1. Since all computations in this paper are carried out in the Lorentz, or hyperboloid, model, we shall use the same symbol Hd to denote both the abstract d-dimensional hyperbolic space and its realization as the upper sheet of the hyperboloid in Rd+1. This mild abuse of notation is standard and causes little ambiguity, because the quantities that enter our model, such as distance, geodesics, barycenters, and probability densities, are intrinsic even when written in ambient coordinates.

>   93: Figure 1 illustrates two equivalent realizations of the same hyperbolic space. The upper sheet of the 2-dimensional hyperboloid $H_{2}$ ⊂ $R_{3}$ is shown together with its stereographic projection from the south pole (0 , 0 , − 1) onto the plane z = 0, yielding the Poincaré disk $B_{2}$ . The red curve on the hyperboloid is a geodesic connecting two points p and q , while the orange dashed segment is the chord in the ambient Euclidean space. This contrast emphasizes that geodesics on H d are determined by the intrinsic hyperbolic metric, not by straight lines in the surrounding Euclidean space. The Poincar´e model is visually intuitive, but the hyperboloid model is computationally preferable here because the distance, exponential map, logarithm map, and tangent-space projection all admit simple formulas with better numerical stability (Mishne et al.; 2023).

Yes—this makes mathematical register a constitutional invariant of the latent manuscript, not merely a formatting rule.

A quick scan of the 23 KisungYou manuscripts makes the problem concrete. Across roughly 1.4 MB of Markdown, I found about 2,839 inline and 1,391 display-math spans, but also approximately 4,665 math-like Unicode glyphs outside those spans in 22 documents. The exact count is heuristic, but the pattern is unmistakable.

For example, [1810.02906v1.md](./bibliotecha/corpora/KisungYou/1810.02906v1.md:32) mixes:

```markdown
$n$ nodes ... matrix A ... n × n ... 1 ≤ i,j ≤ n ... L = D − A
```

Later it fragments one expression as:

```markdown
$c_{1}$ ( t ) = ( $c_{1}$ 1 ( t ) ,...)
```

And [2604.24895v1.md](./bibliotecha/corpora/KisungYou/2604.24895v1.md:74) contains a shattered display beginning with the Unicode expression `⟨x,y⟩L =`, while nearby formulas are properly delimited. This is exactly the intermediate state between visually legible extraction and systematic register capture.

The canonical form should instead use maximal coherent mathematical spans:

```markdown
Let $c_1(t) = (c_{1,1}(t), \ldots, c_{1,N}(t))$ be ...
```

rather than alternating repeatedly between prose and tiny mathematical fragments.

### The lexical contract

I think your standard is converging toward rules like these:

- Inline mathematics is always `$...$`.
- Display mathematics is always isolated within `$$...$$`.
- Mathematical Unicode is forbidden in the encoded manuscript:
  - `α` → `\alpha`
  - `≤` → `\leq`
  - `∈` → `\in`
  - `ℝ` → `\mathbb{R}`
  - mathematical alphanumeric glyphs such as `𝑥` → an appropriate TeX representation
- Mathematical TeX commands never occur outside a math node.
- ASCII identifiers are still math when used mathematically: bare prose `A`, `n`, or `f(x)` must be classified and enclosed even though they contain no special glyphs.
- Punctuation belonging to the sentence normally stays outside the math delimiter: `$x \in X$,` not `$x \in X,$`.
- Dollar signs in prose are escaped.
- Inline math cannot cross a newline; display math has explicit block boundaries.
- Code fences are protected as a distinct register.
- Headings, captions, table cells, list items, and image alt text obey the same math rules as body prose.

“No glyphs” is therefore a necessary lexical rule, but not a sufficient register test. The difficult inference is recognizing that `A` in “matrix A” is a mathematical identifier, while `A` at the beginning of an ordinary sentence is prose.

### A layered native AST

I would separate three levels:

```text
Markdown document AST
└── register nodes
    ├── prose
    ├── inline math
    ├── display math
    ├── code
    └── assets/structural nodes

math register node
└── TeX-like math lexer and AST
    ├── identifiers and numbers
    ├── operators and relations
    ├── groups
    ├── scripts
    ├── commands
    ├── environments
    └── embedded textual phrases
```

For example:

```text
Prose("Let ")
InlineMath(
  source = "c_1(t) = (c_{1,1}(t), \\ldots, c_{1,N}(t))",
  ast = ...
)
Prose(" be a time-dependent vector.")
```

This immediately gives you exact masks. Replacing every math node with a sentinel yields a prose projection; retaining only math nodes yields a mathematical projection in document order. Those projections are derived from parsing, not regex.

There is one important nesting case: `\text{for all}` is prose embedded inside the mathematical register. The document-level mask can treat its containing expression as math, while the math AST retains a `Text` child. That is cleaner than pretending the entire manuscript has only two primitive token types.

### KaTeX versus MathJax

“KaTeX-level” seems like the right abstraction level: syntactic and presentational mathematics, without prematurely attempting a computer-algebra or theorem-prover interpretation. In particular, the AST need not decide whether juxtaposition means multiplication, function application, or something domain-specific.

But I would make the canonical dialect independent of either renderer:

```text
Canonical Math Core
├── KaTeX-compatible TeX vocabulary
└── controlled extensions adopted from MathJax
```

KaTeX and MathJax then become renderer/validation profiles. The standard owns the canonical lexicon and normalization rules, so a future renderer change does not redefine the manuscript language.

### How the converters converge

The LaTeX and PDF routes solve different halves of the same problem:

```text
LaTeX:
explicit register boundaries
→ macro normalization
→ canonical math tokens
→ math AST

PDF:
glyphs + geometry + context
→ register classification
→ glyph-to-token normalization
→ the same math AST
```

The LaTeX exporter is therefore the best environment for discovering the grammar and building trustworthy fixtures. The PDF converter later has to infer both the boundary and the token sequence, but it should never emit glyphs directly into Markdown and hope that a cleanup pass finds them.

An excellent immediate invariant for `latex-ingest` would be:

> The finished manuscript can be parsed into deterministic register spans; every math span parses under the canonical dialect; no mathematical Unicode, TeX math command, or confidently mathematical token remains in prose.

That is stronger and more relevant than merely asking whether KaTeX happens to render the document. It turns the export exercise into the empirical construction of the native Markdown math language you are describing.

> # Context Mode: Default for All Large Output
>
> ## MANDATORY RULE
>
> <context_mode_logic>
>   <mandatory_rule>
>     Default to context-mode for ALL commands. Only use Bash for guaranteed-small-output operations.
>   </mandatory_rule>
> </context_mode_logic>
>
> Bash whitelist (safe to run directly):
> - **File mutations**: `mkdir`, `mv`, `cp`, `rm`, `touch`, `chmod`
> - **Git writes**: `git add`, `git commit`, `git push`, `git checkout`, `git branch`, `git merge`
> - **Navigation**: `cd`, `pwd`, `which`
> - **Process control**: `kill`, `pkill`
> - **Package management**: `npm install`, `npm publish`, `pip install`
> - **Simple output**: `echo`, `printf`
>
> **Everything else → `ctx_execute` or `ctx_execute_file`.** Any command that reads, queries, fetches, lists, logs, tests, builds, diffs, inspects, or calls an external service. This includes ALL CLIs (gh, aws, kubectl, docker, terraform, wrangler, fly, heroku, gcloud, etc.) — there are thousands and we cannot list them all.
>
> **When uncertain, use context-mode.** Every KB of unnecessary context reduces the quality and speed of the entire session.
>
> ## Decision Tree
>
> ```
> About to run a command / read a file / call an API?
> │
> ├── Command is on the Bash whitelist (file mutations, git writes, navigation, echo)?
> │   └── Use Bash
> │
> ├── Output MIGHT be large or you're UNSURE?
> │   └── Use context-mode ctx_execute or ctx_execute_file
> │
> ├── Fetching web documentation or HTML page?
> │   └── Use ctx_fetch_and_index → ctx_search
> │
> ├── Using Playwright (navigate, snapshot, console, network)?
> │   └── ALWAYS use filename parameter to save to file, then:
> │       browser_snapshot(filename) → ctx_index(path) or ctx_execute_file(path)
> │       browser_console_messages(filename) → ctx_execute_file(path)
> │       browser_network_requests(filename) → ctx_execute_file(path)
> │       ⚠ browser_navigate returns a snapshot automatically — ignore it,
> │         use browser_snapshot(filename) for any inspection.
> │       ⚠ Playwright MCP uses a SINGLE browser instance — NOT parallel-safe.
> │         For parallel browser ops, use agent-browser via execute instead.
> │
> ├── Using agent-browser (parallel-safe browser automation)?
> │   └── Run via execute (shell) — each call gets its own subprocess:
> │       execute("agent-browser open example.com && agent-browser snapshot -i -c")
> │       ✓ Supports sessions for isolated browser instances
> │       ✓ Safe for parallel subagent execution
> │       ✓ Lightweight accessibility tree with ref-based interaction
> │
> ├── Processing output from another MCP tool (Context7, GitHub API, etc.)?
> │   ├── Output already in context from a previous tool call?
> │   │   └── Use it directly. Do NOT re-index with ctx_index(content: ...).
> │   ├── Need to search the output multiple times?
> │   │   └── Save to file via ctx_execute, then ctx_index(path) → ctx_search
> │   └── One-shot extraction?
> │       └── Save to file via ctx_execute, then ctx_execute_file(path)
> │
> └── Reading a file to analyze/summarize (not edit)?
>     └── Use ctx_execute_file (file loads into FILE_CONTENT, not context)
> ```
>
> ## When to Use Each Tool
>
> | Situation | Tool | Example |
> |-----------|------|---------|
> | Hit an API endpoint | `ctx_execute` | `fetch('http://localhost:3000/api/orders')` |
> | Run CLI that returns data | `ctx_execute` | `gh pr list`, `aws s3 ls`, `kubectl get pods` |
> | Run tests | `ctx_execute` | `npm test`, `pytest`, `go test ./...` |
> | Git operations | `ctx_execute` | `git log --oneline -50`, `git diff HEAD~5` |
> | Docker/K8s inspection | `ctx_execute` | `docker stats --no-stream`, `kubectl describe pod` |
> | Read a log file | `ctx_execute_file` | Parse access.log, error.log, build output |
> | Read a data file | `ctx_execute_file` | Analyze CSV, JSON, YAML, XML |
> | Read source code to analyze | `ctx_execute_file` | Count functions, find patterns, extract metrics |
> | Fetch web docs | `ctx_fetch_and_index` | Index React/Next.js/Zod docs, then search |
> | Playwright snapshot | `browser_snapshot(filename)` → `ctx_index(path)` → `ctx_search` | Save to file, index server-side, query |
> | Playwright snapshot (one-shot) | `browser_snapshot(filename)` → `ctx_execute_file(path)` | Save to file, extract in sandbox |
> | Playwright console/network | `browser_*(filename)` → `ctx_execute_file(path)` | Save to file, analyze in sandbox |
> | MCP output (already in context) | Use directly | Don't re-index — it's already loaded |
> | MCP output (need multi-query) | `ctx_execute` to save → `ctx_index(path)` → `ctx_search` | Save to file first, index server-side |
> | Wipe indexed KB content | `ctx_purge(confirm: true)` | Permanently deletes all indexed content |
>
> ## Automatic Triggers
>
> Use context-mode for ANY of these, without being asked:
>
> - **API debugging**: "hit this endpoint", "call the API", "check the response", "find the bug in the response"
> - **Log analysis**: "check the logs", "what errors", "read access.log", "debug the 500s"
> - **Test runs**: "run the tests", "check if tests pass", "test suite output"
> - **Git history**: "show recent commits", "git log", "what changed", "diff between branches"
> - **Data inspection**: "look at the CSV", "parse the JSON", "analyze the config"
> - **Infrastructure**: "list containers", "check pods", "S3 buckets", "show running services"
> - **Dependency audit**: "check dependencies", "outdated packages", "security audit"
> - **Build output**: "build the project", "check for warnings", "compile errors"
> - **Code metrics**: "count lines", "find TODOs", "function count", "analyze codebase"
> - **Web docs lookup**: "look up the docs", "check the API reference", "find examples"
>
> ## Language Selection
>
> | Situation | Language | Why |
> |-----------|----------|-----|
> | HTTP/API calls, JSON | `javascript` | Native fetch, JSON.parse, async/await |
> | Data analysis, CSV, stats | `python` | csv, statistics, collections, re |
> | Shell commands with pipes | `shell` | grep, awk, jq, native tools |
> | File pattern matching | `shell` | find, wc, sort, uniq |
>
> ## Search Query Strategy
>
> - BM25 uses **OR semantics** — results matching more terms rank higher automatically
> - Use 2-4 specific technical terms per query
> - **Always use `source` parameter** when multiple docs are indexed to avoid cross-source contamination
>   - Partial match works: `source: "Node"` matches `"Node.js v22 CHANGELOG"`
> - **Always use `queries` array** — batch ALL search questions in ONE call:
>   - `ctx_search(queries: ["transform pipe", "refine superRefine", "coerce codec"], source: "Zod")`
>   - NEVER make multiple separate ctx_search() calls — put all queries in one array
>
> ## External Documentation
>
> - **Always use `ctx_fetch_and_index`** for external docs — NEVER `cat` or `ctx_execute` with local paths for packages you don't own
> - For GitHub-hosted projects, use the raw URL: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/org/repo/main/CHANGELOG.md`
> - After indexing, use the `source` parameter in search to scope results to that specific document
>
> ## Critical Rules
>
> 1. **Always console.log/print your findings.** stdout is all that enters context. No output = wasted call.
> 2. **Write analysis code, not just data dumps.** Don't `console.log(JSON.stringify(data))` — analyze first, print findings.
> 3. **Be specific in output.** Print bug details with IDs, line numbers, exact values — not just counts.
> 4. **For files you need to EDIT**: Use the normal Read tool. context-mode is for analysis, not editing.
> 5. **For Bash whitelist commands only**: Use Bash for file mutations, git writes, navigation, process control, package install, and echo. Everything else goes through context-mode.
> 6. **Never use `ctx_index(content: large_data)`.** Use `ctx_index(path: ...)` to read files server-side. The `content` parameter sends data through context as a tool parameter — use it only for small inline text.
> 7. **Always use `filename` parameter** on Playwright tools (`browser_snapshot`, `browser_console_messages`, `browser_network_requests`). Without it, the full output enters context.
> 8. **Don't re-index data already in context.** If an MCP tool returned data in a previous response, it's already loaded — use it directly or save to file first.
>
> ## Sandboxed Data Workflow
>
> <sandboxed_data_workflow>
>   <critical_rule>
>     When using tools that support saving to a file: ALWAYS use the 'filename' parameter.
>     NEVER return large raw datasets directly to context.
>   </critical_rule>
>   <workflow>
>     LargeDataTool(filename: "path") → mcp__context-mode__ctx_index(path: "path") → ctx_search()
>   </workflow>
> </sandboxed_data_workflow>
>
> This is the universal pattern for context preservation regardless of
> the source tool (Playwright, GitHub API, AWS CLI, etc.).
>
> ## Examples
>
> ### Debug an API endpoint
> ```javascript
> const resp = await fetch('http://localhost:3000/api/orders');
> const { orders } = await resp.json();
>
> const bugs = [];
> const negQty = orders.filter(o => o.quantity < 0);
> if (negQty.length) bugs.push(`Negative qty: ${negQty.map(o => o.id).join(', ')}`);
>
> const nullFields = orders.filter(o => !o.product || !o.customer);
> if (nullFields.length) bugs.push(`Null fields: ${nullFields.map(o => o.id).join(', ')}`);
>
> console.log(`${orders.length} orders, ${bugs.length} bugs found:`);
> bugs.forEach(b => console.log(`- ${b}`));
> ```
>
> ### Analyze test output
> ```shell
> npm test 2>&1
> echo "EXIT=$?"
> ```
>
> ### Check GitHub PRs
> ```shell
> gh pr list --json number,title,state,reviewDecision --jq '.[] | "\(.number) [\(.state)] \(.title) — \(.reviewDecision // "no review")"'
> ```
>
> ### Read and analyze a large file
> ```python
> # FILE_CONTENT is pre-loaded by ctx_execute_file
> import json
> data = json.loads(FILE_CONTENT)
> print(f"Records: {len(data)}")
> # ... analyze and print findings
> ```

> ## Browser & Playwright Integration
>
> **When a task involves Playwright snapshots, screenshots, or page inspection, ALWAYS route through file → sandbox.**
>
> Playwright `browser_snapshot` returns 10K–135K tokens of accessibility tree data. Calling it without `filename` dumps all of that into context. Passing the output to `ctx_index(content: ...)` sends it into context a SECOND time as a parameter. Both are wrong.
>
> **The key insight**: `browser_snapshot` has a `filename` parameter that saves to file instead of returning to context. `ctx_index` has a `path` parameter that reads files server-side. `ctx_execute_file` processes files in a sandbox. **None of these touch context.**
>
> ### Workflow A: Snapshot → File → Index → Search (multiple queries)
>
> ```
> Step 1: browser_snapshot(filename: "/tmp/playwright-snapshot.md")
>         → saves to file, returns ~50B confirmation (NOT 135K tokens)
>
> Step 2: ctx_index(path: "/tmp/playwright-snapshot.md", source: "Playwright snapshot")
>         → reads file SERVER-SIDE, indexes into FTS5, returns ~80B confirmation
>
> Step 3: ctx_search(queries: ["login form email password"], source: "Playwright")
>         → returns only matching chunks (~300B)
> ```
>
> **Total context: ~430B** instead of 270K tokens. Real 99% savings.
>
> ### Workflow B: Snapshot → File → Execute File (one-shot extraction)
>
> ```
> Step 1: browser_snapshot(filename: "/tmp/playwright-snapshot.md")
>         → saves to file, returns ~50B confirmation
>
> Step 2: ctx_execute_file(path: "/tmp/playwright-snapshot.md", language: "javascript", code: "
>           const links = [...FILE_CONTENT.matchAll(/- link \"([^\"]+)\"/g)].map(m => m[1]);
>           const buttons = [...FILE_CONTENT.matchAll(/- button \"([^\"]+)\"/g)].map(m => m[1]);
>           const inputs = [...FILE_CONTENT.matchAll(/- textbox|- checkbox|- radio/g)];
>           console.log('Links:', links.length, '| Buttons:', buttons.length, '| Inputs:', inputs.length);
>           console.log('Navigation:', links.slice(0, 10).join(', '));
>         ")
>         → processes in sandbox, returns ~200B summary
> ```
>
> **Total context: ~250B** instead of 135K tokens.
>
> ### Workflow C: Console & Network (save to file if large)
>
> ```
> browser_console_messages(level: "error", filename: "/tmp/console.md")
> → ctx_execute_file(path: "/tmp/console.md", ...) or ctx_index(path: "/tmp/console.md", ...)
>
> browser_network_requests(includeStatic: false, filename: "/tmp/network.md")
> → ctx_execute_file(path: "/tmp/network.md", ...) or ctx_index(path: "/tmp/network.md", ...)
> ```
>
> ### CRITICAL: Why `filename` + `path` is mandatory
>
> | Approach | Context cost | Correct? |
> |----------|-------------|----------|
> | `browser_snapshot()` → raw into context | **135K tokens** | NO |
> | `browser_snapshot()` → `ctx_index(content: raw)` | **270K tokens** (doubled!) | NO |
> | `browser_snapshot(filename)` → `ctx_index(path)` → `ctx_search` | **~430B** | YES |
> | `browser_snapshot(filename)` → `ctx_execute_file(path)` | **~250B** | YES |
>
> ### Key Rule
>
> > **ALWAYS use `filename` parameter when calling `browser_snapshot`, `browser_console_messages`, or `browser_network_requests`.**
> > Then process via `ctx_index(path: ...)` or `ctx_execute_file(path: ...)` — never `ctx_index(content: ...)`.
> >
> > Data flow: **Playwright → file → server-side read → context**. Never: **Playwright → context → ctx_index(content) → context again**.
>
> ## Subagent Usage
>
> Subagents automatically receive context-mode tool routing via a PreToolUse hook. You do NOT need to manually add tool names to subagent prompts — the hook injects them. Just write natural task descriptions.
>
> ## Anti-Patterns
>
> - Using `curl http://api/endpoint` via Bash → 50KB floods context. Use `ctx_execute` with fetch instead.
> - Using `cat large-file.json` via Bash → entire file in context. Use `ctx_execute_file` instead.
> - Using `gh pr list` via Bash → raw JSON in context. Use `ctx_execute` with `--jq` filter instead.
> - Piping Bash output through `| head -20` → you lose the rest. Use `ctx_execute` to analyze ALL data and print summary.
> - Narrowing `ctx_execute` output upstream of capture → `ctx_execute` captures, `ctx_search` filters; merging the layers drops data that the index never sees. See `references/anti-patterns.md` §8.
> - Running `npm test` via Bash → full test output in context. Use `ctx_execute` to capture and summarize.
> - Calling `browser_snapshot()` WITHOUT `filename` parameter → 135K tokens flood context. **Always** use `browser_snapshot(filename: "/tmp/snap.md")`.
> - Calling `browser_console_messages()` or `browser_network_requests()` WITHOUT `filename` → entire output floods context. **Always** use the `filename` parameter.
> - Passing ANY large data to `ctx_index(content: ...)` → data enters context as a parameter. **Always** use `ctx_index(path: ...)` to read server-side. The `content` parameter should only be used for small inline text you're composing yourself.
> - Calling an MCP tool (Context7 `query-docs`, GitHub API, etc.) then passing the response to `ctx_index(content: response)` → **doubles** context usage. The response is already in context — use it directly or save to file first.
> - Ignoring `browser_navigate` auto-snapshot → navigation response includes a full page snapshot. Don't rely on it for inspection — call `browser_snapshot(filename)` separately.
> - Expecting `ctx_stats` to reset or wipe anything → `ctx_stats` is read-only (shows stats only). Use `ctx_purge(confirm: true)` to permanently delete all indexed content.
>

> ### `run.ps1` imports Pester (>=5) by explicit path anchored on `$env:PORTABLE_ROOT`
>
> `run.ps1` imports Pester (>=5) by explicit path anchored on `$env:PORTABLE_ROOT`
> (`$PORTABLE_ROOT/PowerShell/Modules/Pester`) — needed while the portable-env integration is degraded
> and the default module path only surfaces the ancient system Pester 3.4.0. It exits non-zero on any
> failure (CI-friendly).
>
> --- [current-session | 2026-07-24 06:24 | execute:javascript] ---
> ### if (-not (Get-Module Pester | Where-Object { $_.Version -ge [version]'5.0' })) {
>
> if (-not (Get-Module Pester | Where-Object { $_.Version -ge [version]'5.0' })) {
>     $manifest = $null
>     if ($env:PORTABLE_ROOT) {
>         $proot = Join-Path $env:PORTABLE_ROOT 'PowerShell\Modules\Pester'
>         if (Test-Path -LiteralPath $proot) {
>             $v = Get-ChildItem -LiteralPath $proot -Directory |
>                  Where-Object { ($_.Name -as [version]) -ge [version]'5.0' } |
>                  Sort-Object { [version]$_.Name } -Descending | Select-Object -First 1
>             if ($v) { $manifest = Join-Path $v.FullName 'Pester.psd1' }
>         }
>     }
>     if ($manifest) { Import-Module $manifest -Force }
>     else { Import-Module Pester -MinimumVersion 5.0 -Force }   # fall back to a v5 on the normal path
> }

> i do want to implement the parsing natively if possible, because i do value minimal external dependencies. but maybe this is misguided. please advise

It is not misguided—provided we distinguish a native LaTeX manuscript parser from a complete TeX interpreter.

A complete TeX parser is the wrong target. TeX can redefine control sequences and even alter tokenization through catcodes, so “parsing” arbitrary TeX ultimately requires executing much of TeX. Even Unified LaTeX explicitly describes its PEG parser as making practical assumptions and warns about complicated control-sequence redefinitions. [Unified LaTeX documentation](https://siefkenj.github.io/unified-latex/index.html)

A native parser for conventional academic LaTeX is entirely reasonable and strategically valuable here.

My recommendation is:

> Implement our own lossless, bounded LaTeX compiler frontend, but place the lexer/parser core in a small C# library behind a first-class PowerShell SDK.

That gives us:

- No third-party runtime parser dependency.
- Strongly typed tokens, syntax nodes, spans, enums, and diagnostics.
- Efficient character-level scanning.
- A genuine state-machine lexer and recursive parser.
- PowerShell-native commands, parameters, errors, paths, and result objects.
- Freedom to design the syntax and manuscript models around this project.
- No Node installation or foreign AST leaking into the public contract.

PowerShell 7 already runs on .NET, so this is substantially more native than introducing a JavaScript compiler stack. PowerShell remains the product surface and orchestration layer; C# handles the part for which PowerShell is not especially well suited.

```text
src/tex-export/
├── TexExport.psd1
├── TexExport.psm1
├── Public/
│   ├── Export-TexDocument.ps1
│   └── ConvertFrom-TexSource.ps1
├── Private/
│   ├── Resolve-TexProject.ps1
│   ├── Invoke-TexCompiler.ps1
│   └── Write-TexExportBundle.ps1
├── Compiler/
│   ├── TexExport.Compiler.csproj
│   ├── Lexing/
│   ├── Parsing/
│   ├── Syntax/
│   ├── Semantics/
│   ├── Manuscript/
│   └── Markdown/
└── README.md
```

The native compiler boundary should be deliberately constrained:

1. The lexer recognizes characters, control sequences, groups, comments, whitespace, math shifts, parameters, and verbatim regions without semantic regex rewriting.
2. The syntax parser constructs a lossless tree of groups, commands, environments, inline math, display math, and text.
3. An explicit command-signature registry binds optional and required arguments.
4. Project resolution handles `\input` and `\include` using parsed commands.
5. Semantic passes recognize manuscript constructs such as title, sections, figures, citations, and bibliography.
6. Unknown constructs remain typed generic nodes and produce diagnostics; they never silently disappear.
7. TeX execution is an optional compile-assistance adapter for bibliography generation, counter resolution, and graphic rendering—not the parser architecture.

This avoids pretending that we can statically interpret arbitrary catcode changes, general `\def` programming, or every package ever written. Such inputs can be diagnosed or delegated to an actual TeX engine.

I would not recommend implementing the core parser entirely as ordinary PowerShell functions. It is possible, but typed recursive syntax structures, cursor-heavy lexing, source spans, and high-volume traversal would make the code noisier and easier to compromise. That would work against the engineering standard you just established.

Unified LaTeX can still be useful as an optional development comparator: feed fixtures to both parsers and investigate disagreements. It need not become a production dependency or dictate our AST.

I paused before creating any module files, so there is no partial Node-based scaffold to unwind. My recommended architecture is therefore **C# compiler core + proper PowerShell SDK**. If “native” specifically means PowerShell-only rather than dependency-free within the PowerShell/.NET platform, tell me; it is feasible, but it is not the engineering choice I recommend.

> # Context Mode: Default for All Large Output
>
> ## MANDATORY RULE
>
> <context_mode_logic>
>   <mandatory_rule>
>     Default to context-mode for ALL commands. Only use Bash for guaranteed-small-output operations.
>   </mandatory_rule>
> </context_mode_logic>
>
> Bash whitelist (safe to run directly):
> - **File mutations**: `mkdir`, `mv`, `cp`, `rm`, `touch`, `chmod`
> - **Git writes**: `git add`, `git commit`, `git push`, `git checkout`, `git branch`, `git merge`
> - **Navigation**: `cd`, `pwd`, `which`
> - **Process control**: `kill`, `pkill`
> - **Package management**: `npm install`, `npm publish`, `pip install`
> - **Simple output**: `echo`, `printf`
>
> **Everything else → `ctx_execute` or `ctx_execute_file`.** Any command that reads, queries, fetches, lists, logs, tests, builds, diffs, inspects, or calls an external service. This includes ALL CLIs (gh, aws, kubectl, docker, terraform, wrangler, fly, heroku, gcloud, etc.) — there are thousands and we cannot list them all.
>
> **When uncertain, use context-mode.** Every KB of unnecessary context reduces the quality and speed of the entire session.
>
> ## Decision Tree
>
> ```
> About to run a command / read a file / call an API?
> │
> ├── Command is on the Bash whitelist (file mutations, git writes, navigation, echo)?
> │   └── Use Bash
> │
> ├── Output MIGHT be large or you're UNSURE?
> │   └── Use context-mode ctx_execute or ctx_execute_file
> │
> ├── Fetching web documentation or HTML page?
> │   └── Use ctx_fetch_and_index → ctx_search
> │
> ├── Using Playwright (navigate, snapshot, console, network)?
> │   └── ALWAYS use filename parameter to save to file, then:
> │       browser_snapshot(filename) → ctx_index(path) or ctx_execute_file(path)
> │       browser_console_messages(filename) → ctx_execute_file(path)
> │       browser_network_requests(filename) → ctx_execute_file(path)
> │       ⚠ browser_navigate returns a snapshot automatically — ignore it,
> │         use browser_snapshot(filename) for any inspection.
> │       ⚠ Playwright MCP uses a SINGLE browser instance — NOT parallel-safe.
> │         For parallel browser ops, use agent-browser via execute instead.
> │
> ├── Using agent-browser (parallel-safe browser automation)?
> │   └── Run via execute (shell) — each call gets its own subprocess:
> │       execute("agent-browser open example.com && agent-browser snapshot -i -c")
> │       ✓ Supports sessions for isolated browser instances
> │       ✓ Safe for parallel subagent execution
> │       ✓ Lightweight accessibility tree with ref-based interaction
> │
> ├── Processing output from another MCP tool (Context7, GitHub API, etc.)?
> │   ├── Output already in context from a previous tool call?
> │   │   └── Use it directly. Do NOT re-index with ctx_index(content: ...).
> │   ├── Need to search the output multiple times?
> │   │   └── Save to file via ctx_execute, then ctx_index(path) → ctx_search
> │   └── One-shot extraction?
> │       └── Save to file via ctx_execute, then ctx_execute_file(path)
> │
> └── Reading a file to analyze/summarize (not edit)?
>     └── Use ctx_execute_file (file loads into FILE_CONTENT, not context)
> ```
>
> ## When to Use Each Tool
>
> | Situation | Tool | Example |
> |-----------|------|---------|
> | Hit an API endpoint | `ctx_execute` | `fetch('http://localhost:3000/api/orders')` |
> | Run CLI that returns data | `ctx_execute` | `gh pr list`, `aws s3 ls`, `kubectl get pods` |
> | Run tests | `ctx_execute` | `npm test`, `pytest`, `go test ./...` |
> | Git operations | `ctx_execute` | `git log --oneline -50`, `git diff HEAD~5` |
> | Docker/K8s inspection | `ctx_execute` | `docker stats --no-stream`, `kubectl describe pod` |
> | Read a log file | `ctx_execute_file` | Parse access.log, error.log, build output |
> | Read a data file | `ctx_execute_file` | Analyze CSV, JSON, YAML, XML |
> | Read source code to analyze | `ctx_execute_file` | Count functions, find patterns, extract metrics |
> | Fetch web docs | `ctx_fetch_and_index` | Index React/Next.js/Zod docs, then search |
> | Playwright snapshot | `browser_snapshot(filename)` → `ctx_index(path)` → `ctx_search` | Save to file, index server-side, query |
> | Playwright snapshot (one-shot) | `browser_snapshot(filename)` → `ctx_execute_file(path)` | Save to file, extract in sandbox |
> | Playwright console/network | `browser_*(filename)` → `ctx_execute_file(path)` | Save to file, analyze in sandbox |
> | MCP output (already in context) | Use directly | Don't re-index — it's already loaded |
> | MCP output (need multi-query) | `ctx_execute` to save → `ctx_index(path)` → `ctx_search` | Save to file first, index server-side |
> | Wipe indexed KB content | `ctx_purge(confirm: true)` | Permanently deletes all indexed content |
>
> ## Automatic Triggers
>
> Use context-mode for ANY of these, without being asked:
>
> - **API debugging**: "hit this endpoint", "call the API", "check the response", "find the bug in the response"
> - **Log analysis**: "check the logs", "what errors", "read access.log", "debug the 500s"
> - **Test runs**: "run the tests", "check if tests pass", "test suite output"
> - **Git history**: "show recent commits", "git log", "what changed", "diff between branches"
> - **Data inspection**: "look at the CSV", "parse the JSON", "analyze the config"
> - **Infrastructure**: "list containers", "check pods", "S3 buckets", "show running services"
> - **Dependency audit**: "check dependencies", "outdated packages", "security audit"
> - **Build output**: "build the project", "check for warnings", "compile errors"
> - **Code metrics**: "count lines", "find TODOs", "function count", "analyze codebase"
> - **Web docs lookup**: "look up the docs", "check the API reference", "find examples"
>
> ## Language Selection
>
> | Situation | Language | Why |
> |-----------|----------|-----|
> | HTTP/API calls, JSON | `javascript` | Native fetch, JSON.parse, async/await |
> | Data analysis, CSV, stats | `python` | csv, statistics, collections, re |
> | Shell commands with pipes | `shell` | grep, awk, jq, native tools |
> | File pattern matching | `shell` | find, wc, sort, uniq |
>
> ## Search Query Strategy
>
> - BM25 uses **OR semantics** — results matching more terms rank higher automatically
> - Use 2-4 specific technical terms per query
> - **Always use `source` parameter** when multiple docs are indexed to avoid cross-source contamination
>   - Partial match works: `source: "Node"` matches `"Node.js v22 CHANGELOG"`
> - **Always use `queries` array** — batch ALL search questions in ONE call:
>   - `ctx_search(queries: ["transform pipe", "refine superRefine", "coerce codec"], source: "Zod")`
>   - NEVER make multiple separate ctx_search() calls — put all queries in one array
>
> ## External Documentation
>
> - **Always use `ctx_fetch_and_index`** for external docs — NEVER `cat` or `ctx_execute` with local paths for packages you don't own
> - For GitHub-hosted projects, use the raw URL: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/org/repo/main/CHANGELOG.md`
> - After indexing, use the `source` parameter in search to scope results to that specific document
>
> ## Critical Rules
>
> 1. **Always console.log/print your findings.** stdout is all that enters context. No output = wasted call.
> 2. **Write analysis code, not just data dumps.** Don't `console.log(JSON.stringify(data))` — analyze first, print findings.
> 3. **Be specific in output.** Print bug details with IDs, line numbers, exact values — not just counts.
> 4. **For files you need to EDIT**: Use the normal Read tool. context-mode is for analysis, not editing.
> 5. **For Bash whitelist commands only**: Use Bash for file mutations, git writes, navigation, process control, package install, and echo. Everything else goes through context-mode.
> 6. **Never use `ctx_index(content: large_data)`.** Use `ctx_index(path: ...)` to read files server-side. The `content` parameter sends data through context as a tool parameter — use it only for small inline text.
> 7. **Always use `filename` parameter** on Playwright tools (`browser_snapshot`, `browser_console_messages`, `browser_network_requests`). Without it, the full output enters context.
> 8. **Don't re-index data already in context.** If an MCP tool returned data in a previous response, it's already loaded — use it directly or save to file first.
>
> ## Sandboxed Data Workflow
>
> <sandboxed_data_workflow>
>   <critical_rule>
>     When using tools that support saving to a file: ALWAYS use the 'filename' parameter.
>     NEVER return large raw datasets directly to context.
>   </critical_rule>
>   <workflow>
>     LargeDataTool(filename: "path") → mcp__context-mode__ctx_index(path: "path") → ctx_search()
>   </workflow>
> </sandboxed_data_workflow>
>
> This is the universal pattern for context preservation regardless of
> the source tool (Playwright, GitHub API, AWS CLI, etc.).
>
> ## Examples
>
> ### Debug an API endpoint
> ```javascript
> const resp = await fetch('http://localhost:3000/api/orders');
> const { orders } = await resp.json();
>
> const bugs = [];
> const negQty = orders.filter(o => o.quantity < 0);
> if (negQty.length) bugs.push(`Negative qty: ${negQty.map(o => o.id).join(', ')}`);
>
> const nullFields = orders.filter(o => !o.product || !o.customer);
> if (nullFields.length) bugs.push(`Null fields: ${nullFields.map(o => o.id).join(', ')}`);
>
> console.log(`${orders.length} orders, ${bugs.length} bugs found:`);
> bugs.forEach(b => console.log(`- ${b}`));
> ```
>
> ### Analyze test output
> ```shell
> npm test 2>&1
> echo "EXIT=$?"
> ```
>
> ### Check GitHub PRs
> ```shell
> gh pr list --json number,title,state,reviewDecision --jq '.[] | "\(.number) [\(.state)] \(.title) — \(.reviewDecision // "no review")"'
> ```
>
> ### Read and analyze a large file
> ```python
> # FILE_CONTENT is pre-loaded by ctx_execute_file
> import json
> data = json.loads(FILE_CONTENT)
> print(f"Records: {len(data)}")
> # ... analyze and print findings
> ```
>
> ## Browser & Playwright Integration
>
> **When a task involves Playwright snapshots, screenshots, or page inspection, ALWAYS route through file → sandbox.**
>
> Playwright `browser_snapshot` returns 10K–135K tokens of accessibility tree data. Calling it without `filename` dumps all of that into context. Passing the output to `ctx_index(content: ...)` sends it into context a SECOND time as a parameter. Both are wrong.
>
> **The key insight**: `browser_snapshot` has a `filename` parameter that saves to file instead of returning to context. `ctx_index` has a `path` parameter that reads files server-side. `ctx_execute_file` processes files in a sandbox. **None of these touch context.**
>
> ### Workflow A: Snapshot → File → Index → Search (multiple queries)
>
> ```
> Step 1: browser_snapshot(filename: "/tmp/playwright-snapshot.md")
>         → saves to file, returns ~50B confirmation (NOT 135K tokens)
>
> Step 2: ctx_index(path: "/tmp/playwright-snapshot.md", source: "Playwright snapshot")
>         → reads file SERVER-SIDE, indexes into FTS5, returns ~80B confirmation
>
> Step 3: ctx_search(queries: ["login form email password"], source: "Playwright")
>         → returns only matching chunks (~300B)
> ```
>
> **Total context: ~430B** instead of 270K tokens. Real 99% savings.
>
> ### Workflow B: Snapshot → File → Execute File (one-shot extraction)
>
> ```
> Step 1: browser_snapshot(filename: "/tmp/playwright-snapshot.md")
>         → saves to file, returns ~50B confirmation
>
> Step 2: ctx_execute_file(path: "/tmp/playwright-snapshot.md", language: "javascript", code: "
>           const links = [...FILE_CONTENT.matchAll(/- link \"([^\"]+)\"/g)].map(m => m[1]);
>           const buttons = [...FILE_CONTENT.matchAll(/- button \"([^\"]+)\"/g)].map(m => m[1]);
>           const inputs = [...FILE_CONTENT.matchAll(/- textbox|- checkbox|- radio/g)];
>           console.log('Links:', links.length, '| Buttons:', buttons.length, '| Inputs:', inputs.length);
>           console.log('Navigation:', links.slice(0, 10).join(', '));
>         ")
>         → processes in sandbox, returns ~200B summary
> ```
>
> **Total context: ~250B** instead of 135K tokens.
>
> ### Workflow C: Console & Network (save to file if large)
>
> ```
> browser_console_messages(level: "error", filename: "/tmp/console.md")
> → ctx_execute_file(path: "/tmp/console.md", ...) or ctx_index(path: "/tmp/console.md", ...)
>
> browser_network_requests(includeStatic: false, filename: "/tmp/network.md")
> → ctx_execute_file(path: "/tmp/network.md", ...) or ctx_index(path: "/tmp/network.md", ...)
> ```
>
> ### CRITICAL: Why `filename` + `path` is mandatory
>
> | Approach | Context cost | Correct? |
> |----------|-------------|----------|
> | `browser_snapshot()` → raw into context | **135K tokens** | NO |
> | `browser_snapshot()` → `ctx_index(content: raw)` | **270K tokens** (doubled!) | NO |
> | `browser_snapshot(filename)` → `ctx_index(path)` → `ctx_search` | **~430B** | YES |
> | `browser_snapshot(filename)` → `ctx_execute_file(path)` | **~250B** | YES |
>
> ### Key Rule
>
> > **ALWAYS use `filename` parameter when calling `browser_snapshot`, `browser_console_messages`, or `browser_network_requests`.**
> > Then process via `ctx_index(path: ...)` or `ctx_execute_file(path: ...)` — never `ctx_index(content: ...)`.
> >
> > Data flow: **Playwright → file → server-side read → context**. Never: **Playwright → context → ctx_index(content) → context again**.
>
> ## Subagent Usage
>
> Subagents automatically receive context-mode tool routing via a PreToolUse hook. You do NOT need to manually add tool names to subagent prompts — the hook injects them. Just write natural task descriptions.
>
> ## Anti-Patterns
>
> - Using `curl http://api/endpoint` via Bash → 50KB floods context. Use `ctx_execute` with fetch instead.
> - Using `cat large-file.json` via Bash → entire file in context. Use `ctx_execute_file` instead.
> - Using `gh pr list` via Bash → raw JSON in context. Use `ctx_execute` with `--jq` filter instead.
> - Piping Bash output through `| head -20` → you lose the rest. Use `ctx_execute` to analyze ALL data and print summary.
> - Narrowing `ctx_execute` output upstream of capture → `ctx_execute` captures, `ctx_search` filters; merging the layers drops data that the index never sees. See `references/anti-patterns.md` §8.
> - Running `npm test` via Bash → full test output in context. Use `ctx_execute` to capture and summarize.
> - Calling `browser_snapshot()` WITHOUT `filename` parameter → 135K tokens flood context. **Always** use `browser_snapshot(filename: "/tmp/snap.md")`.
> - Calling `browser_console_messages()` or `browser_network_requests()` WITHOUT `filename` → entire output floods context. **Always** use the `filename` parameter.
> - Passing ANY large data to `ctx_index(content: ...)` → data enters context as a parameter. **Always** use `ctx_index(path: ...)` to read server-side. The `content` parameter should only be used for small inline text you're composing yourself.
> - Calling an MCP tool (Context7 `query-docs`, GitHub API, etc.) then passing the response to `ctx_index(content: response)` → **doubles** context usage. The response is already in context — use it directly or save to file first.
> - Ignoring `browser_navigate` auto-snapshot → navigation response includes a full page snapshot. Don't rely on it for inspection — call `browser_snapshot(filename)` separately.
> - Expecting `ctx_stats` to reset or wipe anything → `ctx_stats` is read-only (shows stats only). Use `ctx_purge(confirm: true)` to permanently delete all indexed content.
>

> Saturday 10:21 PM
> Yes—then I placed the AST one layer too low. pdfdig should produce grounded evidence and candidate math spans; Markpig owns the formal mathematical language, parser, syntax tree, visitors, canonicalization, and renderer projections.
>
> The implied target is something like a canonical embedded mathematical register: a formally specified language island inside a Markdown manuscript.
>
> The missing middle layer
> There are really four distinct objects:
>
> Layer Responsibility
> pdfdig evidence Glyphs, geometry, typography, reading-order hypotheses, provenance and uncertainty
> Manuscript host Markdown structure with explicit, addressable inline/block math spans
> Canonical math surface A versioned, deterministic TeX-like serialization
> Markpig Math AST Tokens, syntax nodes, visitors/rewriters, diagnostics, renderers and equivalence operations
> The canonical surface is not itself the AST. It is the one stable textual representation of an AST—the math equivalent of a formatter’s canonical output.
>
> A host MathSpanSyntax could reference a sibling MathSyntaxTree. A normal Markpig visitor may treat it as an opaque embedded-language node, while a nested visitor explicitly crosses into the math tree. Source maps compose across that boundary:
>
> PDF glyphs → pdfdig span → Markdown MathSpanSyntax
> → Markpig MathSyntaxTree
> → canonical math text
> That gives the PowerShell/Roslyn interop model a clean ownership boundary.
>
> Intersection versus union
> I would not define the language directly as either the intersection or union of LaTeX and MathJax.
>
> MathJax is primarily an input-processing/rendering ecosystem, while LaTeX is a macro-programming and typesetting language. Their literal intersection is too weak; their union inherits macros, package behavior, renderer extensions, ambiguity, and substantial non-mathematical typesetting machinery.
>
> A better construction is:
>
> a closed canonical core grammar;
> versioned extension namespaces for constructs outside the core;
> importers for TeX/LaTeX, MathJax-TeX, perhaps MathML;
> renderer capability profiles such as katex, mathjax, and latex;
> an explicit unsupported or opaque-extension node rather than silent degradation.
> Thus Markpig might accept many source dialects, but serialize one canonical dialect:
>
> parse(source dialect) → Math AST
> canonicalize(AST) → canonical math surface
> lower(AST, renderer) → renderer-specific expression or diagnostic
> The desired invariant is approximately:
>
> parse(serialize(AST)) ≡ AST

>
> Your intuition is closer to a quotient or partial inverse than a conventional converter. Typesetting maps a manuscript into a final-form rendering while discarding or obscuring some semantics. Pdfdig is trying to recover a canonical manuscript modulo presentation:
>

> R

> q

> A(R(m))≈q(m)

> R
> R is typesetting,
> q
> q deliberately forgets pagination, fonts, line wrapping, float placement, and other printing choices, and
> A
